items.prose: A solution set is drawn on the line.
items.question: Which inequality does it show?

options.why: The dot at −3 is filled, so −3 is in. That needs $\ge$.
The bar runs right, towards bigger numbers such as 0. That is greater than.
That reads $x \le -3$, with the bar running left. Read it with $x$ first.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the dot, then the direction.

explain.text: The filled dot keeps −3 in, and the bar runs right to bigger numbers. So the set is $x \ge -3$, which can also be written $-3 \le x$.

options.why: You divided by $-2$ and kept $>$. Test $x = 0$: $6 > 14$ is false.
You added 6 to 14. Subtract 6 from both sides: $-2x > 8$.
Two slips: $8 \div -2 = -4$, and dividing by $-2$ reverses the sign.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract 6, then divide by $-2$ and reverse the sign.

explain.text: Subtract 6: $-2x > 8$. Divide by $-2$ and reverse: $x < -4$. Check $x = -5$: $6 + 10 = 16$, which is bigger than 14.

options.why: You multiplied by $s$. It multiplies $t$, so divide by it.
That is upside down. Dividing $d = st$ by $s$ leaves $d$ on top.
You subtracted $s$. But $s$ multiplies $t$; it is not added.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Undo the multiplication.

explain.text: $t$ is multiplied by $s$, so divide both sides by $s$: $t = \dfrac{d}{s}$. Check: 150 km at 50 km/h takes 3 hours.

items.question: How many whole numbers satisfy it?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract 1 from all three parts, divide by 3, then count.

byKey.took-three: You counted 3. The sign $<$ leaves 3 out.
byKey.dropped-low: You left out −1. The sign $\le$ keeps it in.

explain.text: Subtract 1 throughout: $-3 \le 3x < 9$. Divide by 3: $-1 \le x < 3$. The whole numbers are −1, 0, 1 and 2.

items.prose: You hold a share bought at £31.20. A take-profit order sells it if the price $p$ rises to £34.50 or above.
items.question: Which inequality describes the prices that trigger the sale?

options.why: You left £34.50 out. “Rises to £34.50 or above” includes £34.50.
That is the prices at or below the target, where you keep holding.
You used the entry price. The order waits for £34.50.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Decide whether £34.50 is in, then the direction.

explain.text: “Or above” includes £34.50 itself, so the symbol has a line under it. Higher prices lie to the right: $p \ge 34.50$.

items.prose: A trade closed at £45.60 with a return of −0.05.
items.question: What was the entry price?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $P_0 = \dfrac{P_1}{1 + r}$ with $r = -0.05$.

byKey.times: You added 5% to £45.60. The 5% was measured from the entry, so divide by 0.95.
byKey.off-exit: You took 5% off the exit price. The trade lost money, so the entry was higher: divide by $1 - 0.05$.

items.prose: A trader's position $q$ must stay within $-500 \le q \le 500$ shares. She is short 150, so $q = -150$. Buying $n$ shares makes it $-150 + n$.
items.question: What is the most shares she can buy?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $-150 + n \le 500$ for $n$.

byKey.limit-only: You used the limit alone. She first buys 150 to get flat, then 500 more.
byKey.subtracted: You worked out 500 − 150. Starting below zero, she has further to go: 500 + 150.
byKey.to-flat: 150 only closes the short. She may keep buying up to long 500.

explain.text: Adding 150 to all three parts of $-500 \le -150 + n \le 500$ gives $-350 \le n \le 650$. She can buy up to 650 shares, or sell up to 350.

items.prose: A strategy's profit on $q$ units is $8q - 2000$ pounds. You want a profit: strictly more than £0.00.
items.question: What is the smallest whole number of units that makes a profit?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $8q - 2000 > 0$, then take the next whole number.

byKey.break-even: At 250 units profit is exactly £0.00. That is break-even, and $>$ leaves it out.

explain.text: $8q - 2000 > 0$ gives $8q > 2000$, so $q > 250$. 250 itself makes exactly £0.00, so the smallest profitable size is 251.
